lesson.title: Adams Inherits a Nation Washington Warned Him About
lesson.summary: John Adams's single term as president, from 1797 to 1801, was dominated by the undeclared naval war with France and the party divisions that Washington's Farewell Address had cautioned against just months before he took office.
lesson.body:
John Adams took office as the second president of the United States in March 1797, elected as the Federalist candidate but saddled with a peculiar constitutional quirk, under the original electoral system the runner up became vice president regardless of party, so Adams found himself governing alongside his chief political rival, Thomas Jefferson of the Democratic-Republicans. Adams had served loyally as Washington's vice president for eight years and inherited both the enormous prestige of following Washington and the deep party divisions that Washington's Farewell Address had warned against just months earlier.

Almost immediately, Adams confronted a foreign policy crisis with France. The French government, angry that the United States had signed the Jay Treaty of 1794 improving relations with Britain, began seizing American merchant ships and refused to receive the American minister sent to Paris. Adams dispatched a new commission to negotiate, but when French agents demanded bribes before talks could even begin, in what became known as the XYZ Affair, American opinion turned sharply against France and Adams found himself under pressure to declare full scale war.

Rather than ask Congress for a declaration of war, Adams pursued a middle course, building up the navy and authorizing American ships to fight French vessels in what became known as the Quasi War, an undeclared conflict fought almost entirely at sea between 1798 and 1800. This decision cost Adams politically within his own party, since Hamilton and other High Federalists wanted a larger military buildup and closer alignment with Britain, but Adams resisted, eventually sending a new peace mission that produced the Convention of 1800 and ended the conflict without a formal war.

Domestically, the crisis with France gave Federalists in Congress the votes to pass the Alien and Sedition Acts of 1798, laws that restricted immigrants' rights and criminalized criticism of the government. Adams signed these bills, and though he used the Sedition Act's prosecutorial power more sparingly than some Federalists wanted, the acts proved deeply unpopular and gave Jefferson and Madison an opening to organize opposition through the Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions, arguing the laws were unconstitutional.

By 1800, the Federalist Party had split badly between Adams and Hamilton's supporters, weakening Adams's chances for reelection just as the Alien and Sedition Acts and wartime taxes had eroded his popularity with voters. He lost the election of 1800 to Jefferson, becoming the first president voted out after seeking a second term, though he used his final weeks in office to appoint a wave of Federalist judges, including a new Chief Justice, John Marshall, appointments that would soon produce the landmark case of Marbury v. Madison and give Federalist principles a lasting foothold in the judiciary long after Adams himself had left Washington for his farm in Massachusetts.
